WEDNESDAY MYSTERY SOLVED - it is dance season, not a permanent weekly pattern. Over the full 571-day record Wed looked like a standing +1.66 kWh outlier, but splitting the record by period shows the effect exists ONLY between 2026-01-08 and 2026-05-28 (+5.24 kWh vs Tue/Thu); in the other three periods it is -0.72, -0.13 and +0.33, i.e. nothing. Within that window the MEDIAN gap (+6.09) exceeds the mean gap, so it is every Wednesday, not a few outliers, and outdoor temps match (46.4F vs 44.5F) so it is not weather. The excess is concentrated 3-7 PM, peaking 4-5 PM at +1.4 kWh/hr. CONFIRMATION: Monday is also a dance day and shows the same 3-7PM bump in the same window (Mon 8.23, Wed 10.72 vs Tue 6.67, Thu 6.92); outside the window the Mon+Wed vs Tue+Thu gap is -0.08 kWh, i.e. the effect vanishes entirely. So dance days cost MORE despite the family being out in the evening - the spend is in the pre-dance getting-ready block (laundry, early dinner, showers). Magnitude ~2.7 kWh/dance-day, about $20 per season. Lesson for future analysis: averaging day-of-week over the whole record manufactured a phantom year-round pattern out of a 5-month seasonal one. Always split by period before believing a weekday effect.

OIL HEATER MEASURED (middle daughter's bedroom, started 10/19). Overnight 11pm-6am usage stepped from 4.54 kWh/night (10/05-10/18) to 6.92 kWh/night (10/19-10/24) = +2.38 kWh/night, about 340W average over 7h, $0.45/night or roughly $13/month. CONFOUND CHECKED AND CLEARED: outdoor temp also dropped (58.3F to 50.8F), but the crawlspace heat lamp is NOT the cause - crawlspace temp FELL with the weather (65.9F to 60.6F), so the lamp was not holding it up and therefore was not running. Daytime usage went DOWN 2.94 kWh over the same split because the warm days of 10/13-10/16 (67-69F) had AC running; that drop is AC ending, not related to the heater.

CALIBRATION EVENT #4 - DRYER ONLY, REPLICATE. 2026-10-27 ~5:32 PM, drying the load washed at 1:49 PM. Comparing these two runs tells me how much a dryer figure varies when nothing has actually changed, which sets the error bar on every appliance number in the inventory. Without it I can produce a figure but cannot say whether a difference of, say, 0.4 kWh between two runs is a real effect or just scatter. FULL SET NOW: (1) 10/26 12:40PM washer+dryer, (2) 10/26 5:38PM dryer, (3) 10/27 1:49PM washer, (4) 10/27 5:32PM dryer. Gives direct measurement of each appliance, an additivity check (2+3 vs 1), and a repeatability check (2 vs 4). Load size/wetness will differ between dryer runs - #4 followed a normal wash, #2 followed the 12:40 wash - so some spread between them is genuine variation in the load, not instrument error. Treat the 2-vs-4 gap as an UPPER bound on noise, not a pure one.

LFP GAUGE ARTEFACT - IMPORTANT METHOD NOTE: segment rates between consecutive readings are wildly unstable - 45 W over the first 2.4h, then 20, 38, 34, and finally 6.9 W over the last 15.6h. Seven watts is impossible when the inverter alone draws 15-20. LFP cells have a very flat voltage curve through the middle of their range, so the percentage falls fast near the top then sticks. CONSEQUENCE: never compute a rate from a short window or from segments; only cumulative figures over many hours are usable, and even those may be biased until a full discharge calibrates the gauge. METHOD - MEASURING WITH BATTERY PERCENTAGE. Lessons from the Delta 3/Pro tests. (1) NEVER compute a rate from a short window: 1% is 10.2 Wh on a Delta 3 and 36 Wh on a Pro, so a reading taken just before or after a tick produces a wildly wrong rate. My 2-hour figures swung 18-45 W on loads that never changed. (2) DISCARD THE FIRST INTERVAL - a unit sitting at the top of its range may be a fraction below the displayed figure and tick over almost immediately, which reads as fast consumption. (3) Use windows of 12+ hours; at 14.7 h the quantisation error falls to +/-0.35 W. (4) I ALSO MISREAD A PM TIMESTAMP AS AM and briefly concluded both batteries had gained charge while discharging, then explained the physics of an event that never happened. Check the ordering of readings before interpreting them.

OUTAGE PLANNING - EGO FAN vs FRIDGE: FAN WINS 24 TO 1. Lee asked whether running the small EGO fan to circulate ventless-gas-log heat in a winter outage is worth the battery energy it takes away from refrigeration. It is, overwhelmingly. OPTION A (fan): three EGO packs 2.5+5.0+7.5Ah = ~840Wh, 6W fan on direct DC with NO inverter in the chain = ~140 hours = 5.8 DAYS of continuous circulation. OPTION B (fridge): 840Wh -> EGO inverter (~15W idle + conversion) = 714Wh -> Delta Pro at 96% charge efficiency = 685Wh -> fridge 70W + Pro overhead 40W = 120W battery draw -> 5.7 HOURS of refrigeration. The transfer chain alone loses ~18% before the Pro overhead is counted. LEVERAGE: 6W fan = 20 BTU/hr electrical input, redistributing ~2,722 BTU/hr of ventless-log heat otherwise stranded at the ceiling of the ~700 sq ft open living area = 133x return on its own energy. This makes the EGO fan the single most efficient use of stored energy in the whole system, because it is the only load that runs direct DC with no inversion. COUNTERPOINT IS WEAK: a closed fridge rides ~4 hours on thermal mass anyway, so 5.7 hours of active cooling buys roughly one extra cycle. OUTAGE DOCTRINE: run the fan, set it to winter mode (clockwise, pushing down) which is exactly the stratification case it is for, and do not transfer EGO energy to the Delta Pro for refrigeration.

BEDROOM TWO-WALL COMPARISON - DATA DOES NOT SUPPORT THE THEORY, AND THE TEST IS TOO CONFOUNDED TO TRUST EITHER WAY. Lee noted the placement: HomePod sits bedside against a poorly-insulated exposed Cape Cod wall (cold to the hand in winter); Aqara sits across the room on a dresser against a wall he insulated himself via attic access (feels much warmer). Prediction: bedside should read colder, more so as it gets colder outside. HEADLINE SEEMS TO CONFIRM: across 552 paired readings (2026-07-03 to 2026-11-06) the dresser/Aqara reads warmer in 97% of readings, mean +2.80F, median +2.52F. BUT THE BINNING INVERTS IT - the gap is LARGEST IN HOT WEATHER: 35-45F out = +2.04F; 45-55F = +1.26F; 55-65F = +1.41F; 65-75F = +2.94F; 75-85F = +4.36F; 85F+ = +5.58F. Correlation(outdoor temp, gap) = +0.620. A wall effect would make the bedside WARMER when outdoors is hot, not 5.6F colder - so something actively cools that corner in summer, most likely an AC supply register near the bed, which also explains the gap growing with AC load. THE DECISIVE TEST GOES THE OTHER WAY: same room/air/HVAC, how much does each sensor follow the outdoor daily swing (n=90 days, 5+ readings)? bedside/HomePod mean swing 2.94F, r=+0.038, slope 0.008; dresser/Aqara mean swing 1.66F, r=+0.310, slope 0.039. The INSULATED walls sensor tracks outdoors ~8x more strongly. Overnight (n=106 evening->morning pairs): dresser drops +0.69F, bedside -0.11F (no drop). The bedside swings more in absolute terms but uncorrelated with weather - consistent with occupancy (two bodies radiating a few hundred W) rather than the wall. THREE CONFOUNDS MAKE THIS UNANSWERABLE AS PLACED: (1) different instruments - HomePod is ~2kg of powered electronics, thermally buffered and self-heating with an opaque Apple correction, vs a tiny battery Aqara that tracks air immediately, so comparing their swings compares instruments not walls; (2) unknown baseline offset - in the mild 60-70F null band with HVAC idle the gap is STILL +2.07F (n=176, sd 1.37), so an unknown share of the 2.80F is just the two devices disagreeing; (3) occupancy + possible AC register at the bedside, neither of which the dresser has. EXPERIMENT PROPOSED: relocate the Aqara to the bed wall beside the HomePod for ~5 cold nights, then return it to the dresser - comparing the SAME instrument in two positions kills the instrument confound, with the HomePod held fixed as a reference for whether the room itself changed. If the gap follows LOCATION the wall theory is confirmed; if it follows the DEVICE we have been measuring firmware. CAVEAT TO KEEP: Lees hand on the wall is real data - that is radiant surface temperature, genuinely colder and genuinely affecting comfort, and an air sensor on a dresser may simply not be the instrument that detects it.

GAS LOG RUNNING COST - FAR CHEAPER THAN ASSUMED, DO NOT RATION THEM. Lee assumed outage heating would cost a lot. Regression on 27 gas billing periods: bill = $49.27 fixed + $0.9427 per unit. The $49.27/month is paid regardless, so the MARGINAL cost of burning gas is $0.9427/unit = $0.00909 per 1,000 BTU at ~103,700 BTU/CCF. LOG SET RUNNING COST: 18,000 BTU/hr = $0.16/hr, $1.96 per 12-hr day, $5.89 over a 3-day outage at 12h/day. 25,000 BTU/hr = $0.23/hr, $2.73/day, $8.18. 30,000 BTU/hr = $0.27/hr, $3.27/day, $9.82. Sixteen to thirty cents an hour - the cheapest line item in the entire outage plan. OUTAGE DOCTRINE: do not ration the logs, and the long-burn-beats-short-cycles efficiency argument is thermodynamically true but financially irrelevant at these prices. SIZING CHECK PASSES: unvented appliances want >=50 cu ft per 1,000 BTU/hr; the open 5,600 cu ft supports up to 112,000 BTU/hr, so a typical set is at about a quarter of capacity. The doorless archways are an ASSET here - they are what makes the room suitable for ventless. THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS WATER, NOT MONEY: ventless puts all combustion moisture in the room, ~0.94 lb per 10,000 BTU. At 25,000 BTU/hr that is 2.3 lb/hr, 3.4 gal per 12-hr day, ~10 gal over a 3-day outage, into a sealed cold house - a condensation/mold risk on poorly insulated surfaces (the bedroom knee wall above all), not a comfort issue. MITIGATION: crack a window an inch and cycle rather than running flat out overnight.

GAS LOGS ARE FULLY GRID-INDEPENDENT - 4 AA BATTERIES, NO AC CONNECTION. Lee confirmed the ventless log set is not wired to the grid at all; ignition runs on 4 AA batteries. This makes the logs the MOST RELIABLE heat or power source in the house - more reliable than the Delta Pro, the EGO packs, or anything with an inverter: no grid, no transfer switch, no round-trip losses, no state of charge. Combined with $0.16-0.32/hr running cost, the winter outage heat plan is now the strongest leg of the whole plan. NEW SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE: four AA batteries. ACTIONS: (1) use LITHIUM AA primaries (Energizer Ultimate Lithium or equivalent) not alkaline - ~20 yr shelf life, rated to -40F, and alkalines both lose capacity in cold and leak when left for years in a control compartment, which is exactly the failure that kills the igniter on the morning it is needed; keep a spare set in a labeled bag taped inside the control door or on the mantel, reachable in the dark. (2) DO NOT substitute rechargeable NiMH - 4 x 1.2V = 4.8V against the 6V the module expects; some ignition boards fire on that and some do not, and an outage is the wrong time to discover which. This also rules out the otherwise-appealing idea of topping them off from the Delta Pro. (3) OPEN QUESTION: do the batteries only LIGHT the set, handing off to a thermocouple, or do they hold the valve energized the whole burn? If the latter, battery life scales with BURN HOURS and a multi-day outage with 12-hour burns could exhaust a set - this decides whether one spare set is plenty or three are wanted. Manual will say, or infer from replacement history. (4) Log a dated changelog line at every battery swap to build a real replacement interval instead of guessing.
